idiom_name: Whole role object with exclusive ownership of its parts (language-neutral)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: the Whole is an object that creates its parts, keeps them private and publishes the operations that use them; the Parts are objects with no independent lifecycle that never appear as mutable handles to clients. Two rules carry the pattern. Exclusivity: exactly one whole owns each part, and creation and destruction of parts are the whole's responsibility, so destruction mirrors construction (parts created in order, released in reverse, and a partially built whole releases what it already created). Recursion: because a whole may itself be a part of a larger whole, the same rules apply at every level, and cross-links (part to whole, sibling to sibling) must be non-owning. Ownership is enforced by the host language where one exists (RAII, ownership types, ARC, Dispose/using); everywhere else the convention lives in factory/handle signatures and in the decision not to expose parts at all.
code_sketch:
whole = Whole.create()      # creates its parts, in order
whole.operation(args)       # clients see one interface only
...
whole.destroy()             # releases parts in reverse, then itself
# invariants: one owner per part; a part never escapes or outlives its whole
pitfalls: Exposing internals (returning the part collection or mutable part handles) turns the pattern into a leaky facade.
Creating parts without owning their destruction is a resource leak with extra steps; construction and destruction must be written together.
A part that holds a strong reference back to its whole keeps the whole alive or creates an uncollectable cycle; back-references must be weak or borrowed.

Wrong move: relying on a GC finalizer to release the parts -> finalisation timing is unspecified and never guaranteed, so a whole that is never explicitly closed leaks file handles, connections or locks -> instead give the whole an explicit close/dispose that cascades to its parts (try-with-resources, using, context manager) and treat finalizers only as a backstop.

Wrong move: handing clients the live part collection so they add and remove parts themselves -> owning-side bookkeeping is bypassed and parts escape or are deleted by surprise cascades (e.g. a child yanked from a JPA parent collection triggers orphanRemoval without the whole's validation) -> instead expose only the whole's add/remove operations, which update both sides of the ownership link and check invariants before mutating the collection.
